passage: Tanvir, you asked on the podcast about living at home after college. Okay, I'm Sudha, twenty-one, working at a bank, and every evening my mother asks me the same questions. Where are you going? With whom? What's her father's name? What time exactly? I earn a salary. I pay for the internet. And I still have to report like a schoolgirl. Last week I said, "Ma, I'm an adult," and she looked so lost. She said, "I've known where you are every day for twenty-one years. How do I stop?" I didn't have an answer. I was angry, but I also felt sorry for her. She really doesn't know how to not be in charge.

qa.a: She works at a bank.

qa.a: She seems confused and a little frightened, having been in charge for twenty-one years and not knowing how to change that role.

passage: I'm Vasudha, Pooja's aunt, and I stayed with them last month. Every evening, as Pooja picked up her keys, her father would lower his newspaper. "Where to?" "Out with friends, Papa." "Which friends? Whose car? Why so late?" Pooja is twenty, finishing her final year. She'd answer shortly, then shut the door a little too firmly. Once I heard her mutter, "I'm not ten anymore." After she left, my brother would sit at the window until he saw her come back. I don't know exactly what either of them felt. But he looked like a man holding a rope he didn't know how to release, and she looked like someone tired of being tied to it.

qa.a: It suggests she feels treated like a child and resents having to explain every plan.

qa.a: They could talk calmly about what her father needs to feel at ease, perhaps just a return time, so he can step back and she can feel respected as an adult.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see her brother's evenings?
qa.a: She sees him waiting at the window until Pooja returns, like a man holding on to a role he doesn't know how to let go of.

"Arohi, where are you going?"

"Out, Mumma. With friends."

"Which friends?"

"College friends."

"Names?"

"Mumma, I'm twenty."

"So? I'm still your mother. Names."

"Kriti, Dev, Sameera. Happy?"

"Who is Dev?"

"A friend! From my class!"

"Where are you going?"

"A café in Koregaon Park."

"Which café? What time will you be back? Will Dev drop you?"

"I'll be back when I'm back."

"Arohi!"

"Mumma, I vote. I have a bank account. I'm doing an internship. And you're asking me like I'm in Class 5."

Rukmini opened her mouth, then closed it. She had been asking these questions for twenty years. She didn't know what else to ask.

qa.a: A café in Koregaon Park.

qa.a: Arohi feels frustrated and treated like a child, despite being twenty, voting and doing an internship.

qa.q: What does Rukmini's closing her mouth suggest about her side?
qa.a: It suggests she feels lost and unsure, not knowing how to let go of a role she's held for twenty years.

subtype: Stage 1: Adult child, parent's old role [Actor]
passage:
I moved back home after my second year at college, and within a week, I was fifteen again.

"Charu, where are you going?" "Who is this Varun who keeps calling?" "Why are you back at ten?"

Varun is my lab partner. We're doing a project on water filters. I tried to explain that. Papa just looked at me over his glasses, like I'd said something suspicious.

At the hostel, I'd managed my own money, my own schedule, even a trip to Rishikesh with friends. At home, I had to report every movement like a prisoner on parole.

The worst part was that I could see Papa didn't mean it badly. One night he said, "For twenty years I knew where you were every minute. Now I don't. I don't know how to stop asking."

I didn't know what to say to that. It was the first honest thing either of us had said all summer.

qa.q: What project are Charu and Varun doing?
qa.a: A project on water filters.

qa.q: How did Charu feel being questioned at home?
qa.a: Charu felt frustrated and treated like a child, like a prisoner on parole, after managing independently at the hostel.

qa.q: What turning point does Papa's honest comment open up?
qa.a: It lets them talk openly about how both feel, so they can agree on how much Charu shares as an adult.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa to have Charu home as an adult?
qa.a: He feels unsure and anxious, used to knowing where Charu was every minute and not knowing how to let go.

grounding: Charu, home from college, is questioned about where she goes and whom she meets and feels treated as a child, while her father admits he doesn't know how to let go.

subtype: Stage 1: Adult child, parent's old role [Actor]
passage:
College counsellor's note, Tuesday

Gopika, a second-year student, came in today, tearful. She lives at home with her mother, Usha, and says she has to report every place she goes and every friend she meets. "She calls me four times if I'm late from the library. I'm twenty-one."

She said she loves her mother and feels guilty for being angry. She described her mother as a widow who has "been in charge of everything for twenty years."

We talked about how her mother's questions may come from fear and long habit rather than distrust, and about how Gopika could share some information willingly, which may reduce the questioning.

She agreed to try telling her mother her plans in the morning, before being asked, for two weeks, and to have one calm conversation about what feels respectful to both of them. We will meet again next Tuesday.

— Ms Fernandes, counsellor

qa.q: How many times does Usha call if Gopika is late from the library?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel about her mother's questions?
qa.a: She feels angry and treated like a child, but also guilty because she loves her mother.

qa.q: What approach did the counsellor suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Sharing plans in the morning before being asked and having one calm talk, which may ease Usha's fear and reduce the questioning.

qa.q: What might Usha be feeling, based on what Gopika says?
qa.a: She may feel fearful and unsure how to let go, after twenty years of being in charge of everything alone.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows Gopika, living at home, questioned about where she goes and feeling treated as a child, while her widowed mother struggles to let go.

subtype: Stage 1: Adult child, parent's old role [Actor]
passage:
Saturday, 11:40 p.m.
I'm twenty, and still Papa stood at the door: "Arohi, where are you going? With whom? Whose car? What time back? Send me a photo when you reach." It was coffee with Sharmila. Coffee! Practically in our own colony. I answered everything politely and then sat in the auto feeling about twelve years old. Sharmila said her mother does the same, which helped a bit.
What I can't say to Papa is that I'm doing an internship, handling my own phone bill, managing everything, and at home I'm still his little girl who needs a permission slip.
And yet, when I got back at ten, he was on the sofa pretending to read, and I saw him breathe out. Twenty years of being the one in charge. Maybe he honestly doesn't know how to stop. Maybe neither of us knows what the new rules are.

qa.q: Whom did Arohi meet for coffee?
qa.a: Arohi met Sharmila for coffee.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel sitting in the auto after answering Papa's questions?
qa.a: She felt small and frustrated, about twelve years old, treated like a child despite her internship and managing her own life.

qa.q: What small step could open this up at this stage?
qa.a: Arohi could tell Papa calmly that she understands his worry and suggest a simpler routine, like one message on arrival, so they shape new rules together.

qa.q: What might Papa be feeling as he pretends to read on the sofa?
qa.a: Papa seems relieved when Arohi returns, showing he was anxious; after twenty years in charge he may feel unsure how to let go.

grounding: Shows a young adult living at home being asked for every detail by a parent, feeling treated as a child while the parent struggles to let go.
